newsitem.title: DEMOCRATIC REPUBLIC OF CONGO: World Bank representatives visit new Congo.
newsitem.headline: World Bank representatives visit new Congo.

text.p: A senior World Bank delegation was scheduled to start exploratory talks on Monday with Laurent Kabila's new Congo government on renewing ties severed in 1993 under ousted dictator Mobutu Sese Seko.

The officials, who arrived in the capital Kinshasa at the weekend, said they planned to meet Finance Minister Mawapanga Mwana Nanga in the morning and hoped to see Kabila, bankers and Congo watchers before leaving on Tuesday.

"The purpose of our visit is to listen to how the new government is viewing economic and social development, and where they feel the Bank's advice and support would be useful," Nils Tcheyan, country director for Burundi, Rwanda and the Democratic Republic of the Congo (formerly Zaire), told Reuters.

"It's clear development efforts in the former Zaire didn't work. The new government has inherited an extremely complex situation and I think at this point they have many short-term concerns," he added.
One World Bank concern will be to reschedule repayments on a foreign debt accumulated under Mobutu that stands at around $14 billion.
Mobutu was ousted last month after a seven-month rebellion by Kabila's Alliance and fled into exile.
The Bank suspended structural adjustment loans to Zaire in 1990 and withdrew entirely from the country in 1993 when accumulated debt arrears to the Bank were at $150 million.
The International Monetary Fund, which has yet to make official contact with Kabila, pulled out shortly afterwards.
At the time loans were cut, Bank officials estimated that two thirds of the national budget was being spent on the Presidency and other related political functions.
Further corruption and mismanagement saw the other third scarcely reaching the social sector it was destined for.

Bretton Woods institutions have for years come under strong criticism from opponents of Mobutu's regime both at home and abroad for continuing to lend to the former Zaire long after the extent of mismanagement was exposed.
But so far there has been no sign from major creditors of a willingness to write off part of the vast foreign debt.
Tcheyan said help could be provided if Kabila's government develops sensible economic and social strategies.

"It is difficult to see how they could repudiate the foreign debt. But the fact the funds (provided to Zaire under Mobutu) did not result in development is a serious concern. They will need help in dealing with debt in order to make up for the past," he said.

Congo's finance minister said recently the World Bank and IMF will have to be patient both on arrears and on renewing relations, while the government puts it policies into action and solves its own problems.

The Alliance, in power for just over a month, has yet to spell out a concrete strategy of how they plan to redevelop the country, devastated not only by decades of misrule but also by the recent conflict.
They say, however, that they can finance internally the major projects already announced.
These include a promised renaissance in road-building involving up to 5,500 km of tarred road, and a petrol pipeline to cross Africa's third largest country.
For the moment, analysts consider these projects to be pipe dreams.
However, outside help for redevelopment is on offer on a grand scale should the government persuade international opinion it has sensible policies, Bank officials say.
"If stability and sustainable growth can be achieved in Congo, imagine what the map of Africa would look like to foreign investors," says Tcheyan.
